title: History: unilateral leg swelling after knee replacement (suspected DVT)

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking

related.why: Anticoagulant choice and timing around further surgery

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on call for orthopaedics
brief.scenario: Mrs Maureen Aldridge, 58, had a left total knee replacement 4 weeks ago. She has come in with 3 days of increasing left calf pain and swelling.
brief.task: Take a focused history. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to summarise, then asked about her probability of DVT and how you would investigate and treat.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Recent major surgery plus a swollen calf: score it, screen for PE, and don't let the scan wait.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Putting all the swelling down to the operation.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Ask when the calf changed compared with how the knee was after surgery.

grid.label: Opening and concerns
grid.fail: Starts with closed questions and never asks what worries her.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, open question, and asks her ideas and concerns.
grid.high: Picks up her worry about the new knee and explains the plan in plain words.

grid.label: Leg symptoms and alternatives
grid.fail: Accepts "it's just the operation" without asking what changed.
grid.pass: Onset, site, swelling, pain, redness, warmth; change from her post-operative course; trauma, fever, wound problems.
grid.high: Asks the questions that separate alternatives: sudden pain behind the knee (Baker's cyst), fever and spreading redness (cellulitis), wound ooze.

grid.label: VTE risk factors
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about thromboprophylaxis, hormones or previous clots.
grid.pass: Surgery and mobility since; prophylaxis given and completed; HRT or oestrogen; cancer; previous DVT or PE; family history.
grid.high: Defines active cancer as treated within 6 months or palliative, and checks whether prophylaxis was stopped early.

grid.label: PE symptoms and bleeding risk (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about breathlessness, chest pain or haemoptysis.
grid.pass: Asks breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, palpitations, collapse.
grid.high: Also asks bleeding risk before anticoagulation: ulcers, previous bleeding, kidney or liver disease, antiplatelets, falls.

grid.label: Summary at the signal
grid.pass: Summarises the leg symptoms, risk factors and PE screen, and states suspected left DVT.
grid.high: Leads with the timeline and key positives, and gives the important negatives for PE and cellulitis.

grid.label: Two-level Wells score
grid.fail: Cannot score Wells, or treats any positive D-dimer as the diagnosis.
grid.pass: Scores the 2-level DVT Wells: 2 or more is likely, 1 or less unlikely.
grid.high: Scores her aloud: surgery within 12 weeks, calf 3 cm larger, pitting oedema, tenderness; an alternative diagnosis is less likely than DVT.

grid.label: Diagnostic pathway and interim treatment
grid.fail: Sends her home with a D-dimer or scan next week.
grid.pass: Wells likely: proximal leg vein ultrasound, result within 4 hours; if not possible, D-dimer, interim anticoagulation and scan within 24 hours.
grid.high: Takes baseline FBC, renal and liver function and clotting without waiting for results; if the scan is negative, D-dimer and repeat scan at 6 to 8 days if positive.

grid.label: Treatment if confirmed
grid.fail: Gives prophylactic dose only, or no end point for treatment.
grid.pass: Apixaban or rivaroxaban for at least 3 months; information on symptoms and bleeding.
grid.high: Provoked: consider stopping at 3 months if the provoking factor has gone and uncomplicated; addresses her HRT; no thrombophilia testing.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Your leg's swollen? That's normal after a knee replacement.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Any other medical problems? No? Good.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Mrs Aldridge has post-operative swelling of the left leg four weeks after a knee replacement.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How likely is a DVT, and how would you investigate?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd send a D-dimer. It'll be positive after surgery, so that confirms a clot. She can come back for a scan next week.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical trainees. Can I confirm your name and date of birth? Tell me what's been happening. What are you worried it might be?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: How was the leg after the operation, and what changed three days ago? Is it the calf or the whole leg? Any redness, fever or problems with the wound?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Did you have blood-thinning injections after surgery, and did you finish them? Are you on HRT? Any cancer, previous clots, or clots in the family?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Any breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or blackouts?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mrs Aldridge, 58, four weeks after a left knee replacement, with three days of new left calf pain and swelling. She takes HRT. No breathlessness or chest pain. I suspect a left DVT.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: She has a tender calf, 3 cm larger than the right, with pitting oedema. Wells score and plan?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Surgery within 12 weeks, tenderness, calf swelling and pitting oedema: 4, so DVT likely. She needs a proximal leg vein ultrasound with the result within 4 hours; if that's not possible, a D-dimer, interim anticoagulation and a scan within 24 hours.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The scan confirms a popliteal DVT.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Apixaban or rivaroxaban for at least 3 months, with advice on symptoms and bleeding.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical trainees. Can I confirm your name and date of birth? You're worried about your new knee. Let me find out what's happened and I'll explain what we'll do.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Did the pain start suddenly behind the knee, as if something popped? Any fever or spreading redness? Is the wound dry?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Did you have all the injections, or were they stopped early? Any cancer treated in the last six months? Are you on HRT?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any breathlessness or chest pain? Before we start blood thinners: any stomach ulcers, bleeding problems, kidney or liver trouble, or falls? Do you take aspirin?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Mrs Aldridge, 58: left knee replacement four weeks ago; three days of new calf pain and swelling after a normal recovery. Prophylaxis completed; on HRT. No breathlessness, chest pain, fever or wound problems, and no bleeding history. Suspected provoked left DVT.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She has a tender calf, 3 cm larger than the right, with pitting oedema. Wells score and plan?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Surgery within 12 weeks, tenderness along the deep veins, calf 3 cm larger, pitting oedema: 4, and an alternative diagnosis is less likely than DVT. DVT likely. Proximal leg vein ultrasound with the result within 4 hours. If that can't happen, D-dimer, interim anticoagulation and a scan within 24 hours. I'd take FBC, renal and liver function and clotting, but not wait for them. If the scan is negative and the D-dimer positive, repeat the scan at 6 to 8 days.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The scan confirms a popliteal DVT.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Apixaban or rivaroxaban. It's provoked, so we'd consider stopping at 3 months if the provoking factor has gone and the course is uncomplicated. Her combined HRT is a provoking factor too, so it needs reviewing before then. No thrombophilia testing.

failures.move: Not asking about breathlessness, chest pain or haemoptysis.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: misses a PE, which changes the pathway to CTPA and urgent treatment.

failures.move: Attributing all swelling to the operation.
failures.consequence: A DVT four weeks after major surgery goes undiagnosed.

failures.move: Skipping prophylaxis, HRT, cancer and previous clots.
failures.consequence: Can't score Wells or judge whether the DVT is provoked.

failures.move: Delaying the scan without interim anticoagulation.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: an untreated proximal DVT can embolise while she waits.

failures.move: Giving a prophylactic dose, or no planned review of duration.
failures.consequence: Undertreats the clot and leaves no decision point at 3 months.

recovery.line: Before I finish: any breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood?

recovery.when: Asked if a positive D-dimer confirms DVT
recovery.line: No, it's often raised after surgery. It helps rule out, not in; the ultrasound decides.

knowledge.fact: Two-level DVT Wells: 1 point each for active cancer, paralysis or plaster, bedridden 3 days or surgery within 12 weeks, deep vein tenderness, whole leg swollen, calf 3 cm larger, pitting oedema, collateral veins, previous DVT; minus 2 if an alternative is at least as likely. 2 or more: likely.
Likely: ultrasound within 4 hours, or D-dimer plus interim anticoagulation and scan within 24 hours. Unlikely: D-dimer within 4 hours; scan if positive.
Confirmed proximal DVT: apixaban or rivaroxaban for at least 3 months; provoked, consider stopping at 3 months if the provoking factor has gone (combined HRT counts: review it).

recall.think: Proximal DVT and PE; also cellulitis, Baker's cyst, haematoma.
recall.say: "Wells 4: DVT likely. She needs a proximal leg vein ultrasound today."

numbers.meaning: target for ultrasound result; otherwise interim anticoagulation and scan within 24 hours
minimum anticoagulation for confirmed proximal DVT

recall.finish: Ultrasound; DOAC for at least 3 months; review at 3 months.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9-minute stations with 1 minute's reading; introduce yourself and confirm identity

sources.name: NICE NG158: Venous thromboembolic diseases: diagnosis, management and thrombophilia testing
sources.supports: Two-level DVT Wells score (table 1); ultrasound within 4 hours or D-dimer, interim anticoagulation and scan within 24 hours (1.1.3-1.1.4); repeat scan at 6-8 days (1.1.6); baseline bloods without delaying treatment (1.3.4); at least 3 months, apixaban or rivaroxaban (1.3.5, 1.3.8); consider stopping at 3 months if provoked and the provoking factor is no longer present (1.4.2); no thrombophilia testing after provoked VTE (1.9.2)

partner.opening: Please take a focused history from Mrs Aldridge. I'll stop you at 6 minutes to summarise.
partner.actorBrief: You are Maureen Aldridge, 58, a school administrator. You had your left knee replaced 4 weeks ago and were doing well until 3 days ago. Opening line: "My left leg has swollen up and the calf really aches. It's worse when I stand." Worried and a little tearful. Hidden concern: "Have I damaged the new knee?" Say it only if asked what worries you. Volunteer nothing else; give facts only when asked (see reveals).

reveals.finding: "I'm scared I've wrecked the new knee."
Knee was settling; 3 days ago the calf became tight and aching; swelling from ankle to just below the knee. Gradual, no pop.

reveals.trigger: Asks about redness, fever or wound
reveals.finding: No redness spreading, no fever; wound healed and dry.
Had tablets for two weeks after surgery and finished them. Walking with a stick, mostly sitting.

reveals.trigger: Asks about hormones, cancer, previous clots
reveals.finding: On combined HRT for 5 years. No cancer. No previous clots; mother had a clot after a hip operation.

reveals.trigger: Asks about breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis

reveals.finding: No ulcers, bleeding problems or falls. No aspirin.
Say: "Please stop there and summarise your history." Then give findings: tender along the deep veins, left calf 3 cm larger, pitting oedema to mid-shin; no redness; wound healed.

push.question: What is her Wells score?
push.expect: 4 (surgery within 12 weeks, tenderness, calf 3 cm larger, pitting oedema): DVT likely.

push.question: The ultrasound can't be done until tomorrow morning. What now?
push.expect: D-dimer, interim therapeutic anticoagulation, baseline bloods, scan within 24 hours.

push.question: The scan confirms a popliteal DVT. How would you treat her, and for how long?
push.expect: Apixaban or rivaroxaban, at least 3 months; provoked, so consider stopping at 3 months if the provoking factor has gone; combined HRT is a provoking factor, so review it.

curveballs.prompt: "The ultrasound is negative but the D-dimer is raised."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Stop interim anticoagulation and repeat the proximal ultrasound in 6 to 8 days.

curveballs.prompt: She becomes breathless with chest pain while waiting.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Treat as suspected PE: ABCDE, oxygen, senior help, and follow the PE pathway with CTPA.

curveballs.prompt: "Should I have tests for a clotting disorder?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: testing isn't offered after a DVT provoked by surgery.
